presentingComplaint: Rapidly spreading, painful red rash over the left shin with fever and chills for 2 days
history: Two days of a sharply advancing, bright-red, hot patch on the left lower leg preceded by 12 hours of high fever and rigors. Reports a small interdigital fissure from chronic tinea pedis as the likely portal of entry. Background of lower-limb lymphoedema after prior cellulitis and mild venous insufficiency. No trauma, no animal/water exposure, no diabetes, no immunosuppression. No breathlessness, chest or abdominal symptoms.
examination: Well-demarcated, raised, indurated erythematous plaque over the anteromedial left shin with a clear step-off from normal skin (peau d'orange texture), warm and tender, with early superficial blistering at the leading edge. Tender left inguinal lymphadenopathy and a faint lymphangitic streak. Interdigital maceration/fissuring present. No crepitus, no dusky discolouration, no bullae with skin necrosis, pain proportionate to appearance (not out of proportion). Alert, not toxic.
imaging: Not indicated for typical erysipelas; bedside ultrasound (if performed) shows subcutaneous oedema/cobblestoning without a drainable collection or fascial fluid tracking
microbiology: Blood cultures sent (positive in <5% of cases); surface swab not recommended. Group A beta-haemolytic Streptococcus (S. pyogenes) is the predominant cause
finalDiagnosis: Erysipelas (Group A streptococcal) of the left lower leg
citations: Harrison 22e — Skin and Soft-Tissue Infections (Cellulitis and Erysipelas)
IDSA Practice Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Management of Skin and Soft Tissue Infections 2014
stewardship: Empiric penicillin-class therapy targeting beta-haemolytic streptococci: oral/IV penicillin V or amoxicillin (IV benzylpenicillin if febrile/systemic); non-purulent, non-severe SSTI does not need routine MRSA cover per IDSA 2014. Elevate limb, treat tinea pedis to remove portal of entry.
contraindications: Penicillin allergy — substitute clindamycin or a macrolide (note rising macrolide resistance in S. pyogenes)
Reduce/adjust renally cleared beta-lactam doses only if significant renal impairment
Avoid unnecessary broad-spectrum/anti-MRSA agents in classic non-purulent erysipelas
edgeCases: Facial ('butterfly') erysipelas can mimic other facial dermatoses; recurrent erysipelas in a lymphoedematous limb may warrant prophylactic penicillin
Failure to improve or pain out of proportion, crepitus, or haemorrhagic bullae must trigger urgent reassessment for necrotizing fasciitis
expectedMaiK: Classic Group A streptococcal erysipelas: a sharply demarcated, raised, rapidly spreading erythema with systemic fever/rigors and a skin portal of entry (tinea pedis). First-line therapy is a penicillin targeting beta-haemolytic streptococci; MRSA cover is not routinely needed for non-purulent erysipelas.
expectedNextQuestions: Is the border sharply demarcated/raised distinguishing it from cellulitis, and is pain out of proportion (red flag for necrotizing infection)?
Is there a portal of entry (tinea pedis, fissure, lymphoedema) or prior episodes suggesting recurrence?
expectedInvestigations: Mark the erythema border and reassess; ultrasound only if abscess or DVT suspected

investigations: Mark erythema border; ultrasound if abscess/DVT suspected
